passage: In the workshop of a small-town polytechnic, Madhav slapped the table. "A sensor is smarter. A float switch is just a stick!" Shankar folded his arms. "A stick that has worked in our village tank for ten years." Their groupmate Bindu suggested they test both in the tank behind the workshop and count how many times each one failed in twenty tries. The float failed once. The sensor, in the dusty water, failed six times. Madhav kept looking at the numbers. He wanted to argue, and did not. The group voted for the float switch. "Fine," he said. "But I'm adding a small buzzer with my circuit." Shankar grinned. "Deal."

qa.q: How many times did the sensor fail in twenty tries?
qa.a: The sensor failed six times.

qa.q: What did Madhav want to do after seeing the numbers, and what did he do instead?
qa.a: He wanted to argue but did not, showing he still disagreed inside yet accepted the data and the vote.

qa.q: How did testing both ideas help the group?
qa.a: Counting failures in the same tank gave everyone facts instead of opinions, so the vote was easier to accept. 🙂

qa.q: How might Shankar see Madhav's offer of the buzzer?
qa.a: Shankar probably sees it as a friendly way to keep Madhav's idea in, since he grinned and agreed.

grounding: A groupmate disagrees strongly on the approach, tests ideas with data and accepts the group's decision.

passage: In the group room at the library in Uppsala, Ingrid had already typed the whole outline and given out the sections in her own order. "This is fine, right?" she said, not waiting. Astrid's jaw tightened. In earlier meetings she had nodded and gone quiet to avoid a quarrel, and her ideas had never made it in. This time she opened the shared document. "I looked at the marking guide. Section three needs a comparison, and I can write it. Let's put who does which part in the document, with dates, so everyone can see." Ingrid paused, then typed Astrid's name next to section three. "Okay. Add the dates."

qa.q: Where did Ingrid and Astrid meet to work?
qa.a: They met in the group room at the library in Uppsala.

qa.q: Why had Astrid gone quiet in earlier meetings?
qa.a: Astrid wanted to avoid a quarrel, so she nodded and stayed silent, though her ideas never made it in.

qa.q: What worked in how Astrid spoke up this time?
qa.a: She pointed to the marking guide and asked for the tasks and dates in the shared document, using facts and writing instead of an argument. 🙂

qa.q: How might Ingrid see Astrid's request?
qa.a: Ingrid paused, then agreed, which suggests she may not have noticed how much she had decided alone.

grounding: One member controls everything; the other speaks with facts and gets tasks shared in writing.

passage: Disha handed Mehak the village-survey questionnaire on the bus to the college in the kasba, and her stomach fluttered. It was the part she had planned for weeks. "Let's look at your first ten forms on Wednesday," Disha said, "and again on Friday." Mehak nodded. Twice that week Disha's fingers hovered over her phone to ask if it was done. She put it down. On Wednesday the forms had gaps in three answers. "These are good. Could we make the age question clearer?" Mehak laughed. "I noticed that too." By Friday the sheet was tidy.

qa.q: When did Disha and Mehak agree to look at the first ten forms?
qa.a: They agreed to look at them on Wednesday.

qa.q: What was Disha feeling as she handed over the questionnaire?
qa.a: Her stomach fluttered, showing nervous hope, since it was the part she had planned for weeks.

qa.q: How did the checkpoints help the group?
qa.a: They gave fixed times to review the work, so Disha did not have to keep asking and Mehak could fix the gaps early.

qa.q: How might Mehak feel about how Disha gave feedback?
qa.a: Mehak probably felt trusted, since Disha praised the forms first and asked kindly about the age question.

grounding: A groupmate hands over a part and hopes it is done well, agreeing checkpoints and giving kind feedback without micromanaging.

passage:
Monday. Kalyani watched Ritu explain the lab results so clearly that even the teacher wrote it down. Kalyani kept her own half-finished graphs closed under her notebook. "Mine aren't ready," she said.

Thursday. She stayed back after class. "How did you make your graphs so easy to read?" Ritu showed her two tricks. Kalyani felt a small sting of envy, but she wrote both down.

Next Tuesday. Kalyani shared her graphs with the group. They were not as sharp as Ritu's, but the axis labels were clear. Ritu smiled. "Yours make my section easier to follow."

qa.q: What did Kalyani say when she hid her graphs on Monday?
qa.a: She said, "Mine aren't ready."

qa.q: What was Kalyani feeling on Thursday when she asked Ritu for help?
qa.a: She felt a small sting of envy but still wanted to learn, so she wrote both tricks down.

qa.q: What changed in how Kalyani handled her work between Monday and Tuesday?
qa.a: She stopped hiding it, learned from Ritu and shared her own graphs with clear labels.

qa.q: How might Ritu see being asked for tricks?
qa.a: Ritu probably feels respected, and her comment that Kalyani's graphs help her section shows the group benefits.

grounding: A groupmate who is better than the protagonist prompts envy, but she learns from them and does her own part.

passage:
"Saurabh, you missed your bus for me last night."
"There's another at eight. It's fine."
"It isn't nothing. You spent two hours on my charts." Sonali held out her notes. "Thank you. I can't fix your slides, but I can take the notes for Thursday's session, and I'll bring chai."
Saurabh scratched his ear. "You don't have to."
"I want to. Yesterday I nearly gave up on the whole chart section, and then you sat down and asked me one question at a time until it made sense. And next week, tell me what you're stuck on. I mean it. 🙏"
"Okay. Chai with less sugar, then."
"Done."

qa.q: How long did Saurabh spend on Sonali's charts?
qa.a: Saurabh spent two hours on Sonali's charts.

qa.q: Why does Sonali insist that it isn't nothing?
qa.a: Sonali feels deeply grateful, because Saurabh missed his bus and spent two hours on her charts, and she wants him to know it mattered.

qa.q: How does Sonali give something back?
qa.a: She offers to take the notes for Thursday's session, bring chai and help when Saurabh is stuck next week.

qa.q: How might Saurabh feel about Sonali's thanks?
qa.a: Saurabh scratches his ear and says she doesn't have to, which suggests he is a little shy but pleased.

grounding: A groupmate stayed late to help; the receiver thanks them and offers help in return.

passage:
Subject: About our project grade

Hi Zainab,

I have been thinking about the grade since Friday. I know my data section was two days late, and that slowed all of us. I am sorry for that part, and I take it as mine. I do not think it is fair to say the whole grade came from that, though, because the conclusions also needed extra analysis that none of us had time for.

Could we meet on Thursday and write down what we will change next time? I am thinking earlier check-ins, a shared plan with dates, and a clear owner for each part. I will bring my notes.

Rehana

qa.q: How late was Rehana's data section?
qa.a: It was two days late.

qa.q: How does Rehana feel about the blame, and what shows it?
qa.a: Rehana feels sorry and responsible for the late data section, but also feels it is unfair for the whole grade to rest on that.

qa.q: What does Rehana propose to do about the poor grade?
qa.a: Rehana proposes a Thursday meeting to write down changes, such as earlier check-ins, a shared plan with dates and a clear owner for each part. 🙂

qa.q: How might Zainab feel on reading the email?
qa.a: Zainab may feel relieved to see Rehana own a share of the problem and focus on next steps rather than an argument.

grounding: After a poor group grade, the protagonist takes responsibility for their own part without taking all the blame.

passage: Counselling note, Tuesday. Vikas came in because his friend Deepak stopped replying three weeks ago, without a word. He said he felt confused and small, and he kept checking his phone during our talk. He told me he had sent many messages and had not stopped rereading the last ones. We talked about how someone's silence can be about their own reasons, not about Vikas's worth. I did not tell him what Deepak thinks, because I do not know. He said the hardest part is never getting an answer. We agreed that he would stop sending messages for now, leave the phone in his bag at cricket practice on Saturday, and come back next week to tell me how it went. I will check in then.

qa.q: How long ago did Deepak stop replying?
qa.a: Deepak stopped replying three weeks ago.

qa.q: What did Vikas feel, and what shows it?
qa.a: Vikas felt confused and small, and he kept checking his phone and rereading the last messages.

qa.q: What did Vikas and the counsellor agree that he would do next?
qa.a: Stop sending messages for now, leave the phone in his bag at cricket practice on Saturday and come back to report.

qa.q: Why did the counsellor avoid saying what Deepak thinks?
qa.a: The counsellor does not know Deepak's reasons, and guessing could pull Vikas further into chasing answers.

grounding: A person is ghosted, feels confused and small and accepts he may never get answers instead of chasing.

passage: I sit next to Jahnavi at our study group. For two weeks I saw her turn her phone face down whenever Tara's messages came in. She didn't look angry, more tense, like someone holding her breath. Tara asked me twice if I knew what she had done wrong. I said I didn't. I don't know what was in Jahnavi's mind. Maybe the talk felt too hard to start. Yesterday Jahnavi typed something short and sent it. She showed me: "I'm sorry I went quiet. It was hard to say I want to work alone this time. Can we talk on Friday?" Her shoulders dropped after. Tara sent a thumbs-up within a minute. Rafiq

qa.q: How long did Rafiq see Jahnavi turn her phone face down?
qa.a: Rafiq saw it for two weeks.

qa.q: What might Jahnavi have been feeling, according to Rafiq's account?
qa.a: She seemed tense rather than angry, and Rafiq thinks the talk may have felt too hard to start, though Rafiq cannot be sure.

qa.q: Why was Jahnavi's short message kinder than more silence?
qa.a: It told Tara that the quiet was not about Tara's mistakes and offered a talk, so Tara no longer had to guess. 🙂

qa.q: How might Tara have felt during the two weeks?
qa.a: Tara asked twice what she had done wrong, so Tara was probably worried and confused.

grounding: A person avoids someone because a talk feels hard, then sends a short honest message instead of vanishing.

subtype: Friend × Being ghosted by a friend [Receiver]
passage: Sit, Nirmala. I'm Gurpreet, and you asked why I never chase people who go quiet, so I will tell you about my closest friend, Harjit. For months she stopped answering my calls. No fight, no reason. I wanted to send angry messages and put something sharp on my status, and my thumb was on the button more than once. I didn't. I wrote one warm message: "I miss you, and I'm here if you ever want to talk." Nothing came back. It hurt for a long time. But I stopped waiting by the phone, and I kept the door open in my heart, not in my inbox. Harjit never answered, and I have made peace with that, and I still smile at our old photographs.

qa.q: How many warm messages did Gurpreet send Harjit?
qa.a: Gurpreet sent one warm message.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet want to do when Harjit went quiet, and what did Gurpreet do instead?
qa.a: Gurpreet wanted to send angry messages and post something sharp, but wrote one warm message and then stopped waiting.

qa.q: What can Nirmala learn about handling a friend who disappears?
qa.a: Send one kind message, then let go if there is no answer, instead of accusing or posting about it publicly.

qa.q: How might Harjit's silence look from Harjit's side?
qa.a: It may have come from Harjit's own reasons that Gurpreet never learned, so it does not prove Gurpreet did wrong.

grounding: A close friend disappears for months; the wise response is one warm message and letting go if there is no answer.

passage: Rain drummed on the tin roof in a small town in Mizoram. Lalremsiami had read her last message to Zoram so many times that she knew it by heart: "Maybe I talked too much about my exams." He had not replied for nineteen days. On Saturday at the tea stall she told Shalini everything. "You have said that line to me three times," Shalini said gently. "Did you insult him? No. It is just a loop." Lalremsiami laughed weakly. That night she wrote in her notebook: "I said nothing wrong. He did not answer. I am allowed to close this myself." She put the phone in the drawer and slept.

qa.q: How many days had Zoram not replied?
qa.a: He had not replied for nineteen days.

qa.q: How was Lalremsiami feeling as she kept rereading her last message?
qa.a: She was anxious and blaming herself, rereading it until she knew it by heart as if she had said something wrong.

qa.q: What steps helped Lalremsiami get out of the loop?
qa.a: She talked to Shalini, heard the loop named, wrote down that she said nothing wrong and put the phone away.

qa.q: How does Shalini see Lalremsiami's repeated line?
qa.a: Shalini sees it as a loop, not proof of a mistake, and answers gently by asking if there was any insult.

grounding: After being ghosted the person replays what she said, notices the loop, talks to a friend and gives herself closure.
